title: Why Teacher Evaluation Reforms Haven't Worked--And How They Can
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler examines two decades of test-based teacher evaluation reform and concludes that the billions spent produced no discernible gains. She opens with the historical parallel of 1890s New York City, where nearly every teacher was rated good, and shows the same pattern recurring after the Obama-era incentives. Her central argument is that linking evaluation to reading scores pushes schools toward generic comprehension-skills practice at the expense of the science and social studies content that actually builds the knowledge and vocabulary tests assume. She adds that evaluation cannot work when teachers are trained in methods that conflict with the science of learning. The piece closes by redirecting the money toward knowledge-building curricula and coaching delivered by people whose job is to support rather than evaluate teachers. It is a compact statement of the knowledge-rich curriculum case applied to teacher quality policy.
points: Test-based teacher evaluation, backed by an estimated $15 to 20 billion, showed no discernible effect on achievement, graduation or college enrollment, and virtually all teachers were still rated satisfactory.
Tying evaluations to reading scores is counter-productive because it rewards skills practice on easy, random-topic texts and squeezes out the content subjects that build vocabulary.
Orthodox teacher training often conflicts with cognitive science, so even a rigorous evaluation system cannot improve results if it judges teachers against ineffective methods.

Wexler proposes spending on science-aligned curricula plus ongoing coaching from someone who knows the materials and supports rather than evaluates, claiming comparable effects to replacing an average teacher with a highly effective one.
quotes: But a recent comprehensive study finds that on balance, none of this worked. Looking at 44 states and Washington, D.C., the researchers analyzed whether “high-stakes” teacher evaluation reforms boosted student test scores, high school graduation rates, or college enrollment.

That’s pretty much what happened back in the 1890s when a new superintendent tried to reform New York City’s evaluation system, as recounted in Dana Goldstein’s The Teacher Wars. He instituted an A to D scale, but the vast majority of teachers still routinely got a B+. The New York Times declared the reform “a joke.

Schools and teachers increase the time kids spend practicing comprehension “skills,” like “making inferences”—the kind of skills that standardized reading tests purport to measure—using easy texts on random topics. As a result, they spend less time on social studies and science.
That can produce short-term gains, but it’s likely to lead to long-term failure. As grade levels go up, tests assume increasing amounts of academic vocabulary.

Scientists who study the learning process, however, have found that having factual information in long-term memory is what enables people to think critically. If teachers are using methods that science has found are unlikely to work, as many are—and if they’re also being evaluated by people trained to believe in those methods—an evaluation system won’t be able to boost student achievement, no matter how rigorous it is.

That suggests that the best way to improve teacher quality is to give teachers instructional materials that can work and ongoing coaching in how to use them—delivered by someone intimately familiar with those materials, whose job is to support teachers rather than evaluate them.

We do need to evaluate teachers’ performance in the classroom, but it’s unfair—and ineffective—to do that when we’re also asking them to use methods that don’t work. And tying evaluations to tests that have nothing to do with the substance of what’s been taught is both counter-productive and unfair to teachers.
